rows.themeProjectDescription:
This project aims to combine swarm intelligence algorithms with machine learning/deep learning models to solve complex time-series forecasting problems in communication or IoT systems.

The student will first investigate standard time-series ML models (e.g., Extreme Learning Machine, Support Vector Regression, or recurrent neural networks). Subsequently, the student will program (using Python) a meta-heuristic optimization algorithm to autonomously search for the optimal hyperparameters of the predictive model, establishing a hybrid "Algorithm-Optimized ML" framework. The proposed framework will be validated using publicly available network traffic or IoT sensor datasets. By comparing the optimized model with traditional baseline models, the student will analyze its superiority in prediction accuracy, convergence speed, and generalization capability.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Hyperspectral remote sensing images contain hundreds of spectral bands, which often introduce high redundancy and increase computational complexity in classification tasks. This project aims to investigate spectral feature selection methods using the Grey Wolf Optimization (GWO) algorithm for hyperspectral image analysis.

The project will focus on selecting representative spectral bands to improve classification accuracy while reducing feature dimensionality. Public hyperspectral datasets such as Indian Pines and Salinas will be used for experimental evaluation. Different classifiers including Support Vector Machine (SVM) and K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) will be employed to compare classification performance before and after feature selection.

A simple visualization and evaluation platform will also be developed in Python to demonstrate selected bands, classification accuracy, and comparison results. The proposed framework is expected to improve feature selection efficiency and reduce redundant spectral information in hyperspectral datasets.

Background

Blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂) is a core indicator for cardiovascular health monitoring. Traditional fingertip-clamping measurement methods have limitations such as restricted usage scenarios and inability to provide continuous monitoring. PPG (Photoplethysmograph) technology, with its advantages of being non-invasive, low-cost, and easy to integrate, has become the mainstream technology path for wearable blood oxygen monitoring. Currently, PPG blood oxygen monitoring faces technical bottlenecks such as motion artifacts, skin color differences, and low power consumption requirements. There is still room for improvement in the measurement accuracy of existing algorithms in complex scenarios. Cutting-edge technologies such as multi-wavelength sensing, polarized light technology, and transfer learning provide new solutions to break through the performance bottlenecks of PPG blood oxygen monitoring.


Main task

1. PPG blood oxygen monitoring principle and sensor selection

1) Conduct an in-depth study on the spectrophotometric principle of PPG blood oxygen measurement, and analyze the sensitivity of different wavelengths of light to blood oxygen saturation.

2) Compare the performance parameters of mainstream PPG sensors (such as MAX30102) and select an appropriate sensor to build a hardware platform.


2. Research on PPG signal preprocessing and anti-interference algorithms

1) Design signal preprocessing algorithms targeting motion artifacts and ambient light interference, including adaptive filtering, wavelet transform, etc.

2) Research signal enhancement methods based on polarization technology to improve the accuracy of blood oxygen measurement for people of different skin colors.


3. Optimization of blood oxygen saturation calculation algorithm

1) Improve the traditional R-value calculation method and combine it with machine learning algorithms to enhance the accuracy of blood oxygen saturation estimation.

2) Research on a rapid calibration method based on transfer learning to achieve quick adaptation of devices across different individuals.


4. Verification of system implementation and performance evaluation

1) Build a wearable device prototype based on STM32/ESP32, integrate algorithms, and conduct performance testing.

2) Test the system from dimensions such as accuracy, response time, and power consumption.


Expected outcomes

Blood oxygen saturation model, system demo
rows.themeTitle: Optimization of blood oxygen saturation measurement algorithm and system implementation for PPG sensor

Background

Cardiovascular disease has become the leading cause of death globally. Traditional electrocardiography (ECG) requires skin contact, posing discomfort and infection risks. Ballistocardiography (BCG) achieves noninvasive and contactless heart monitoring by capturing the micro-vibrations on the body surface caused by heart beats. However, traditional acquisition methods suffer from insufficient sensitivity. Flexible fiber optic sensing technology, with its advantages such as high sensitivity, resistance to electromagnetic interference, and good biocompatibility, provides a new technological path for BCG signal acquisition.


Main task

1. BCG signal preprocessing and feature extraction

1) Research on signal preprocessing algorithms: Aimed at the noise and interference present in BCG signals, we investigate effective signal preprocessing algorithms, including filtering, denoising, baseline drift correction, etc., to enhance signal quality.

2) Research on feature extraction methods: Extract feature information related to physiological parameters from preprocessed BCG signals, including time-domain features (such as peak values, valley values, intervals), frequency-domain features (such as power spectrum, spectral entropy), and time-frequency domain features (such as wavelet transform coefficients).

3) Feature selection and optimization: Select and optimize the extracted features, choosing those with the highest discriminability for physiological parameters to enhance the performance of subsequent algorithms.

2. Research on physiological parameter analysis algorithm based on BCG signals

1) Heart rate and respiratory rate estimation algorithms: Research on heart rate and respiratory rate estimation algorithms based on BCG signals, including traditional time-domain analysis methods, frequency-domain analysis methods, and machine learning-based methods, to improve the accuracy and robustness of the estimation algorithms.

2) Blood pressure estimation algorithm: Explore blood pressure estimation algorithms based on BCG signals, establish a mathematical model between BCG signal characteristics and blood pressure, and achieve non-invasive and continuous monitoring of blood pressure.

3) Analysis of other physiological parameters: Research on analysis methods for other physiological parameters (such as vascular elasticity, heart rate variability) based on BCG signals, expanding the application scope of BCG signals.

3. Algorithm verification

Collect a large amount of BCG signal data and corresponding physiological parameter data to validate the proposed algorithm and evaluate its performance metrics (such as accuracy, recall rate, F1 score, etc.)


Expected outcomes: Physiological parameter model
rows.themeTitle: Physiological parameter analysis based on flexible fiber optic BCG signals

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) is a non-invasive, high-resolution ophthalmic imaging technique widely used for fundus disease screening and clinical diagnosis. It serves as a reliable basis for intelligent analysis of retinal lesions. However, due to inherent imaging mechanisms and biological tissue scattering effects, raw OCT images are easily contaminated by severe speckle noise. Such noise obscures subtle retinal structural details, interferes with lesion observation, and degrades the accuracy of subsequent intelligent diagnosis and quantitative analysis. Traditional denoising methods tend to over-smooth textures while eliminating noise, failing to balance noise suppression and detail preservation, which greatly restricts their practical application in high-precision ophthalmic image processing.


Aiming at the above defects, this graduation project investigates an effective OCT image denoising method based on diffusion model and attractor network. The main task is to construct a targeted intelligent denoising model for ophthalmic OCT images. By integrating the strong noise fitting ability of the diffusion model and the stable feature extraction advantage of the attractor network, the optimized model is designed to suppress complex speckle noise adaptively.


This study is expected to effectively remove speckle noise from OCT images while preserving critical retinal structures and lesion details. The proposed method can achieve a better trade-off between denoising performance and detail retention than conventional algorithms. It can significantly improve the overall quality of original OCT images, provide high-quality data support for subsequent fundus lesion analysis and intelligent diagnosis, and offer a feasible technical reference for ophthalmic medical image preprocessing.
rows.themeTitle: Research on Denoising Model of Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) Images

1) Background

With the aging global population and the increasing number of empty-nest elderly living alone, the demand for intelligent home monitoring systems has grown significantly. Traditional surveillance cameras often require high bandwidth for cloud processing and raise privacy concerns due to continuous video streaming. Furthermore, many existing solutions rely on cloud-based Artificial Intelligence (AI), which introduces latency and depends heavily on network stability.


Recent advancements in Edge AI (Artificial Intelligence on the device) allow complex computer vision tasks—such as human detection, pose estimation, and behavior analysis—to be processed locally on low-cost hardware. Integrated smart camera modules (e.g., reCamera Gimbal series based on the SG2002 chipset) now combine high-resolution imaging, pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) mechanical control, and dedicated Neural Processing Units (NPUs, up to 1 TOPS) into a single, compact device. This enables real-time, localized monitoring without sending sensitive data to the cloud, providing a robust platform for developing privacy-first, responsive safety applications for the elderly or vulnerable individuals.


2) Main Task

The primary objective of this project is to develop a standalone smart monitoring system deployed entirely on an edge AI camera. The student is expected to implement the following core functionalities:


  • Embedded Linux & Development Environment Setup:​ Configure the edge computing board (e.g., reCamera Gimbal 2002), establish SSH connectivity, and set up the cross-compilation environment for deploying AI models to the NPU.

  • Real-time Human Detection & Tracking:​ Implement a lightweight object detection algorithm (e.g., YOLOv5n or YOLOv8n) to identify humans in the video stream. Develop a control logic that utilizes the camera's integrated PTZ (Pan-Tilt-Zoom) API to automatically track the detected person, keeping them centered in the frame.

  • Abnormal Behavior (Fall) Detection:​ Deploy a secondary model or logic for fall detection. This involves analyzing the aspect ratio of the bounding box (width/height) or utilizing a lightweight pose estimation model (e.g., MoveNet) to detect sudden changes in posture indicative of a fall or collapse.

  • Alert Notification System:​ Implement a network communication module using standard protocols (HTTP/HTTPS). Upon detecting an abnormal event, the system must send a real-time alert notification (including timestamp and snapshot) to a designated WeChat account via the WeChat Work API or a similar push service.

  • System Integration:​ Optimize the application to run efficiently within the resource constraints of the edge device (memory, CPU, NPU), ensuring stable, long-term operation without external computational support.

3) Expected Outcomes

Upon completion of the project, the student is expected to deliver:


  • Functional Prototype:​ A fully operational physical prototype consisting of the integrated edge AI camera. The device should autonomously detect a human subject, track their movement via the PTZ mechanism, identify simulated falls, and trigger a WeChat alert.

  • Source Code & Documentation:​ Complete source code for the embedded application, including the detection/tracking algorithms and the network notification script, along with a README file detailing the build and deployment process.

  • Final Report (Dissertation):​ A comprehensive technical report (typically 60-80 pages) covering:


  • Literature review of Edge AI and computer vision for healthcare.

  • Detailed system architecture and hardware/software specifications.

  • Methodology of model selection, quantization (INT8), and deployment on the NPU.

  • Experimental results demonstrating the system's real-time performance (FPS) and accuracy in various indoor scenarios.

  • Demonstration Video:​ A short video showcasing the end-to-end functionality: "Human enters room -> Camera tracks -> Subject simulates fall -> WeChat alert received on mobile phone."
rows.themeTitle: Design of an Embedded AI-Based Smart Home Monitoring System with Abnormal Behavior Detection and Alerting

Age-related Macular Degeneration (AMD) is a common blinding eye disease that seriously endangers the visual health of the elderly. At present, color fundus photography and optical coherence tomography serve as the core clinical imaging tools for AMD evaluation and diagnosis. Traditional AMD diagnosis relies on manual observation and judgment by ophthalmologists, which is inefficient and prone to subjective deviation. With the rapid development of intelligent medical technology, deep learning has become an effective means to assist ophthalmic disease diagnosis. However, clinical fundus image data often faces the problem of insufficient labeled samples, which restricts the construction and application of high-precision AMD diagnosis models.

This graduation project carries out targeted research on intelligent auxiliary diagnosis of AMD. Two core research tasks are defined in this study. Firstly, an AMD classification model suitable for small sample scenarios is constructed to realize intelligent identification of AMD types and severity, providing reliable classification basis for clinical diagnosis. Secondly, a deep semantic segmentation model is applied and optimized to identify and segment key AMD markers, so as to accurately obtain the specific location, scope and structural feature information of lesion markers.

It is expected that the proposed model can achieve accurate AMD classification and stable marker segmentation under small sample conditions. The research can effectively make up for the shortcomings of traditional manual diagnosis, reduce clinical diagnosis workload and improve the efficiency and objectivity of AMD screening. The research results provide a feasible technical scheme for the intelligent auxiliary diagnosis of AMD, and offer valuable reference for the popularization of intelligent ophthalmic diagnosis systems in primary clinical scenarios.
rows.themeTitle: Research on Auxiliary Diagnosis of Age-Related Macular Degeneration Based on Disease Classification and Marker Segmentation

Fundus optic disc and optic cup segmentation is a core and essential task in intelligent medical diagnosis, which provides critical technical support for the auxiliary diagnosis and clinical treatment of glaucoma and other ophthalmic diseases. With the rapid development of deep learning, deep semantic segmentation technology can realize end-to-end feature learning of fundus images and complete high-precision segmentation of optic disc and optic cup regions. Nevertheless, existing segmentation methods still have certain defects in practical clinical application. It is difficult to accurately fit the blurred contour boundaries of optic disc and cup, and the model shows poor stability when facing complex and diverse clinical fundus data. Meanwhile, most models fail to fully mine lesion feature information and achieve quantitative calculation of diagnostic parameters, which limits the intelligent level of glaucoma auxiliary diagnosis systems.

This graduation project focuses on the above pain points and sets three core research tasks. Firstly, the study optimizes the segmentation algorithm to enhance the accurate recognition ability of optic disc and optic cup contour boundaries. Secondly, relevant improvement strategies are adopted to strengthen the model’s adaptive stability for different types of clinical fundus data. Thirdly, this research explores the internal lesion feature rules of segmented fundus images and realizes quantitative measurement of key diagnostic parameters for glaucoma screening.

It is expected that the improved semantic segmentation model proposed in this project can achieve more accurate boundary segmentation of optic disc and optic cup. The optimized model will possess stronger generalization ability and clinical data adaptability. In addition, this study can realize effective mining of fundus lesion features and reliable quantitative calculation of diagnostic parameters. The research results can effectively assist the intelligent screening of glaucoma, providing a reliable technical reference for the popularization and application of intelligent ophthalmic auxiliary diagnosis systems.
rows.themeTitle: Research on Optic Disc and Optic Cup Segmentation of Fundus Based on Deep Semantic Segmentation Technology

Deep neural networks have been widely applied in intelligent perception and image recognition fields due to their powerful feature extraction capabilities. However, the complex network structure of conventional deep learning models leads to redundant parameters, high computational costs and low inference efficiency, which severely limits the deployment of models on low-computing devices such as mobile terminals and embedded devices. In intelligent healthcare and fundus image diagnosis scenarios, bulky segmentation models are difficult to apply in real-time and portable clinical screening, restricting the practical promotion of medical auxiliary diagnosis systems. Aiming at the above problems, this graduation project carries out research on network lightweight optimization oriented to retinal vessel segmentation.

The main research task is to explore an efficient redundant parameter discrimination mechanism for segmentation networks. On the premise of guaranteeing the segmentation accuracy and generalization ability of the original model, the research prunes redundant neurons and weight parameters of the network to streamline the overall network structure. This method is adopted to effectively reduce the model’s computational complexity and storage overhead, solving the problem of high resource consumption of traditional segmentation models.

It is expected that the lightweight model constructed in this project can maintain excellent retinal blood vessel segmentation performance while significantly reducing parameter quantity and inference time. The optimized model will possess lower hardware dependence and better portability, realizing efficient and accurate segmentation of fundus images in low-computing scenarios. This study provides a practical technical solution for the lightweight deployment of intelligent medical diagnosis models and lays a foundation for the popularization of portable fundus screening equipment.
rows.themeTitle: Research on Lightweight Method of Deep Neural Network Based on Pruning Optimization

1. Background


This task adopts a public dataset specially

designed for retail multi-step prediction on the Kaggle platform, which is

dedicated to time series multi-horizon forecasting in the retail industry.

Constructed for retail commodity sales scenarios, the dataset contains

multidimensional temporal and static features, including historical sales

volume, date and time attributes, holiday labels, promotional activities, as

well as store and commodity properties.

 


It features multi-commodity and multi-store

records with long-span continuous time sampling, covering real business

conditions such as regular sales, holiday fluctuations, and promotion-induced

disturbances. The dataset presents obvious temporal trends and periodicity with

comprehensive feature dimensions and standardized sample partitioning. It can

be adapted to multi-step time series forecasting modeling without extensive

data reconstruction, and fully meets the task requirements of multi-interval

sales prediction in the retail industry.

 


2. Main task


This scheme takes the Temporal Fusion

Transformer (TFT) architecture as the core backbone. For the multi-step time

series prediction scenario in retail sales, targeting the problems of retail

data such as temporal dependence, heterogeneous features, strong disturbances

from holidays and promotions, and difficulties in multi-horizon joint

prediction, the scheme first conducts preprocessing including temporal feature

encoding, categorical feature embedding, as well as cleaning and normalization

of missing values and outliers.

 


Relying on the unique gating mechanism,

attention layers and temporal fusion modules of TFT, it adaptively captures

both long-term and short-term temporal dependencies, and conducts hierarchical

fusion modeling on static attribute features, continuous temporal features and

categorical temporal features.

 


3. Expected outcomes


Through the global attention mechanism, key

historical time nodes are selected to weaken the interference of noise and

irrelevant features, supporting the one-time output of prediction results for

multiple future time steps. Combined with classic error metrics for time series

prediction to carry out quantitative evaluation, the scheme achieves

high-precision and interpretable multi-horizon time series sales prediction for

retail commodities.

1. Background


This task uses a public dataset dedicated

to multi-sensor time series on the Kaggle platform, which is specially designed

for multi-source sensor time series classification and sequence modeling. The

dataset integrates data collected from three types of devices: IMU (Inertial

Measurement Unit), THM (Temperature Sensor), and TOF (Time-of-Flight) sensor.

It contains multi-dimensional continuous time-series features such as

acceleration, angular velocity, temperature and distance.

 


The data is sampled regularly in

chronological order with good multi-sensor time synchronization and stable

sampling frequency. It covers continuous time-series sampling samples under

different scenarios. Featuring rich data dimensions, unified sequence length,

and noise distribution consistent with real acquisition environments, the

dataset is well partitioned and requires no complex alignment preprocessing. It

is well suited for deep learning-based tasks of multi-sensor time series

recognition, classification and sequence modeling.

 


2. Main task


This scheme takes BiLSTM (Bidirectional

Long Short-Term Memory) and GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit) combined with the

attention mechanism as the core backbone architecture. Aiming at the

characteristics of multi-sensor time series data, such as strong temporal

dependence, high feature dimensionality and scattered key information, the

scheme firstly performs data preprocessing including cleaning, normalization

and time series slicing on multi-source sensing data of IMU, THM and TOF.

 


BiLSTM and GRU are adopted to

bidirectionally mine the forward and backward temporal dependencies, and

capture both long-term and short-term evolutionary features of sensor

sequences. On this basis, the attention mechanism is introduced to adaptively

assign weights, focus on critical time segments and important sensing features,

weaken the interference of redundant noise, and enhance the representation of

effective features.

 


3. Expected outcomes


Relying on the hierarchical feature

extraction and end-to-end training mode of deep learning, the deep mining and

modeling of multi-sensor time series features are completed. Common evaluation

indicators for classification tasks are used for quantitative performance

verification, so as to realize high-precision time series recognition and

modeling analysis under multi-sensor fusion.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background


This task adopts the public dataset dedicated to book recommendation

systems from the Kaggle platform. The dataset is specially constructed for the

scenario of personalized book recommendation based on graph neural networks,

and it belongs to the user-item interaction recommendation dataset. Its core

consists of three major dimensions: user ID, book ID, and users’ rating

interaction records on books. Meanwhile, it is attached with auxiliary data

such as basic book metadata and user behavior interaction logs. The data

reflects real implicit and explicit user behavioral feedback on books.

 


The interaction relationships between users and books are dense with

sufficient interaction samples, without severe problems of data sparsity and

imbalance. The bipartite graph structure of users and books is clear and

well-organized, and the topological relationship of the graph structure can be

constructed without complex preprocessing, which well meets the task

requirements of graph convolution-based collaborative filtering recommendation

algorithms.

 


2. Main task


Taking the lightweight graph convolutional network as the core

backbone architecture, the proposed scheme abandons the nonlinear

transformation and redundant feature layers in traditional graph convolutional

networks, and only retains the pure graph convolutional neighborhood

aggregation mechanism to adapt to the user-item bipartite graph structure of

the recommendation system. It propagates high-order neighborhood interaction

information of users and books layer by layer through multi-layer graph

convolution, mines users' latent preferences and correlation features of books,

and generates low-dimensional dense user embeddings and book embeddings. Rating

prediction and similarity matching are implemented based on the inner product

of embedding vectors to realize personalized book recommendation.

 


3. Expected outcomes


The model models high-order collaborative filtering signals relying

on the graph structure, simplifies the network architecture and reduces

computational complexity. Meanwhile, it eliminates redundant feature

transformations to avoid overfitting, and focuses on mining the topological

interaction relationships between users and books. It is applicable to the cold

start and personalized matching scenarios of book recommendation. Quantitative

evaluation and performance verification of the model are completed using

commonly adopted evaluation metrics for recommendation systems.

Measurement of signal distortion degree is crucial for ensuring the performance and reliability of signal processing systems, and it is an indispensable part in fields such as electronics, communications, and audio-video processing.

d) Display the input signal THD value measured by the measuring device, the one-period waveform, and the normalized amplitude of the fundamental and harmonic waves.

3. Expected outcomes

a) Prototype circuit for Signal distortion measurement device;

b) Complete design report and source code.

2. Main Tasks

d. Develop a PC control interface (using LabVIEW/Matlab) to adjust parameters via UART, ensuring both PC and local controls are valid simultaneously.

A fully functional FPGA-based signal generator prototype with dual-control capability, supporting three waveforms, adjustable amplitude and frequency, buzzer feedback, and OLED display. A complete test report and graduation thesis documenting the design and implementation process are also required.

1. Background

Convolutional neural networks are widely used in image recognition and embedded artificial intelligence. Although CNN inference is computationally intensive, its convolution and matrix-vector operations can be accelerated using FPGA parallelism and on-chip memory. Handwritten digit recognition using a simplified LeNet-style network provides a controlled and well-understood task for undergraduate FPGA design. This project focuses on fixed-point quantisation, RTL implementation of core CNN layers, memory scheduling, and board-level demonstration of digit classification.


2. Main Task

(1) Research CNN inference, LeNet or simplified CNN structures, fixed-point quantisation, and FPGA neural-network accelerators; select a network size and layer structure that can fit within target FPGA resources.

(2) Train the selected model on the MNIST dataset using Python, then export weights, biases, test images, and intermediate layer outputs as reference files for RTL verification.

(3) Develop a fixed-point quantisation scheme for input pixels, weights, biases, accumulators, and feature maps. Compare floating-point and fixed-point accuracy to confirm acceptable approximation error.

(4) Design image, weight, bias, and feature-map storage using ROM or BRAM. Address-generation logic shall provide correct data access for convolution, pooling, and fully connected layers.

(5) Design the convolution window and multiply-accumulate module. The module shall read feature-map windows, perform multiple multiplications and accumulations, add bias, and apply truncation or saturation.

(6) Design activation, pooling, and feature-map buffering modules. ReLU shall clamp negative values to zero; pooling shall perform max or average pooling; buffers shall pass layer outputs to the next layer.

(7) Design fully connected and classification modules. The circuit shall calculate ten class scores, select the maximum score as the predicted digit from 0 to 9, and output the result via display or UART.

(8) Construct layer-by-layer SystemVerilog testbenches comparing RTL outputs with Python reference results, then demonstrate stored or UART-input digit samples on FPGA and report accuracy, resources, and frequency.


3. Expected Outcomes

Deliverables include a synthesizable lightweight CNN inference RTL codebase covering image buffering, weight storage, convolution, activation, pooling, fully connected, classification, and control modules. Verification outputs will include layer-by-layer comparison logs, quantisation-error analysis, classification results, resource reports, and board demonstration evidence. The thesis will present CNN theory, training and quantisation methods, hardware architecture, storage scheduling, accuracy/resource trade-offs, and experimental records.

1. Background

Digital oscilloscopes and spectrum analysers are essential tools in electronic measurement and signal analysis. Their core functions involve sampling, buffering, triggering, waveform display, and frequency-domain transformation. Implementing a simplified oscilloscope on FPGA allows students to combine digital signal processing theory with real-time hardware design. By using an internal DDS as a controllable signal source, the project can be completed without relying on an external ADC, while still providing a clear time-domain and frequency-domain board demonstration.


2. Main Task

(1) Research sampling theory, quantisation error, DDS signal generation, trigger-based waveform display, fixed-point FFT, and spectrum visualisation; define sampling depth, display resolution, FFT length, and refresh-rate requirements.

(2) Design a DDS signal source using a phase accumulator, frequency control word, and waveform lookup table. The system shall generate sine, square, and triangular test signals.

(3) Design a parameter configuration module using buttons, switches, or UART to control waveform type, frequency control word, amplitude scale, trigger level, and time/frequency display mode.

(4) Implement a sampling buffer using dual-port RAM or FIFO. The module shall store continuous samples and resolve the rate difference between the sampling side and the display side.

(5) Design trigger-control logic to detect rising-edge or falling-edge crossings around a configurable trigger level, lock the trigger point, and read samples before and after the trigger.

(6) Design the time-domain display module. Sample values shall be mapped to screen y-coordinates, sample indices to x-coordinates, and axes, grids, waveform points, or line segments shall be rendered.

(7) Design FFT processing and spectrum display. A fixed-length sample window shall be transformed using FFT IP or a fixed-point FFT module, and magnitude results shall be converted into spectrum bars with peak-bin detection.

(8) Construct testbenches to verify DDS frequency, trigger location, FFT peak position, amplitude mapping, and display coordinates; demonstrate waveform switching, frequency adjustment, and time/frequency display switching on FPGA.

Deliverables include a synthesizable RTL system containing DDS, sampling buffer, trigger control, time-domain waveform display, FFT processing, spectrum rendering, and user-control modules. The verification report will include simulation waveforms, FFT reference comparisons, resource utilisation, timing results, and board demonstration evidence. 1. Background

AES-128 is a widely adopted symmetric encryption standard used in secure communication, data storage, and embedded security systems. Its round-based structure, finite-field arithmetic, and well-defined standard test vectors make it well suited for FPGA-based hardware acceleration and verification. Compared with software implementation, a hardware AES core can provide higher throughput and deterministic latency. This project focuses on the RTL design of an AES-128 encryption/decryption accelerator, including key expansion, round transformations, control logic, and a simple communication interface for board-level demonstration.


2. Main Task

(1) Research the AES-128 standard, including 128-bit block structure, 10-round encryption, decryption flow, SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, AddRoundKey, and key expansion rules.

(2) Define the 128-bit data interface and 4x4 state-matrix byte ordering. This mapping shall be documented clearly to avoid byte-order errors in the RTL implementation.

(3) Design S-box and inverse S-box modules. Each module shall accept an 8-bit byte and output the substituted byte; ROM lookup may be used as the baseline implementation.

(4) Design MixColumns and InvMixColumns modules. GF(2^8) multiplication by 2, 3, 9, 11, 13, and 14 shall be implemented and linked to the mathematical derivation.

(5) Implement the key expansion module using RotWord, SubWord, Rcon, and XOR operations to generate all required round keys for encryption and decryption.

(6) Develop encryption and decryption datapaths. The design shall implement the correct round sequence, including the initial round, normal rounds, and final round differences.

(7) Design a control FSM and UART/register interface to manage input loading, round counting, mode selection, done indication, result buffering, plaintext/key input, and ciphertext/plaintext output.

(8) Verify the design using NIST standard test vectors and report encryption/decryption correctness, simulation waveforms, latency, throughput, resource utilisation, maximum frequency, and FPGA serial demonstration results.


3. Expected Outcomes

Deliverables include a fully synthesizable AES-128 RTL codebase containing S-boxes, column-mixing units, key expansion, round control, communication interface, and verification testbenches. A verification report will provide standard-vector comparison results, simulation waveforms, performance metrics, and FPGA serial demonstration evidence. The thesis will cover AES theory, finite-field derivation, hardware architecture, performance analysis, verification procedure, and engineering records.

1. Background

Lightweight embedded processors are fundamental building blocks in modern SoCs and digital integrated circuits. The open RISC-V instruction set provides a clear and accessible architecture for studying processor datapaths, control logic, memory access, and peripheral integration. Building a small RV32I-compatible processor on FPGA allows students to connect instruction-set theory with synthesizable RTL design and board-level demonstration. This project focuses on the design of a single-cycle or multi-cycle RV32I processor core and its integration with simple memory-mapped peripherals.


2. Main Task

(1) Research the RV32I instruction set and define a feasible instruction subset covering arithmetic, logic, load/store, branch, and jump instructions; prepare an instruction support table and project schedule.

(2) Design the overall CPU datapath, including PC update, instruction fetch, instruction decode, immediate generation, register file, ALU, data memory access, and write-back selection.

(3) Implement the instruction fetch and PC update module. It shall support reset entry, PC+4 sequential execution, conditional branch target selection, and JAL/JALR jump target selection.

(4) Implement instruction decode and immediate generation. The decoder shall output register addresses, immediate values, ALU operation codes, memory access type, branch/jump control, and write-back type.

(5) Design the register file and ALU. The register file shall support two read ports and one write port with x0 fixed to zero; the ALU shall support arithmetic, logic, shift, and comparison operations.

(6) Design data memory access and write-back logic. The system shall support word/half-word/byte load-store operations, sign extension, memory write enable control, and selection among ALU, memory, and PC+4 write-back data.

(7) Design on-chip memory and memory-mapped peripherals, such as GPIO, Timer, UART, or seven-segment display registers, so that software can control external outputs through load/store instructions.

(8) Develop assembly test programs and automated testbenches to check register values, RAM contents, branch behaviour, peripheral outputs, and FPGA board demonstration through LEDs, seven-segment display, or UART.


3. Expected Outcomes

Deliverables include a synthesizable RV32I lightweight processor RTL project with CPU core, on-chip ROM/RAM, address decoder, and basic peripherals. Verification materials will include assembly test programs, simulation waveforms, automated result checks, and FPGA board demonstration results. The final thesis will describe the RISC-V ISA analysis, datapath and controller design, peripheral mapping, verification strategy, project planning, engineering logs, and board-level testing.

1. Background

Real-time image processing is widely used in machine vision, industrial inspection, intelligent transportation, and embedded perception systems. Edge detection extracts object contours and structural information from images and is a representative algorithm for demonstrating how software image-processing methods can be mapped onto parallel hardware pipelines. Compared with CPU-based offline processing, FPGA implementation can process pixel streams with low latency by using line buffers, shift registers, and parallel arithmetic units. This project focuses on the RTL design of a Sobel-based image edge detection pipeline and a target region annotation unit, with VGA/HDMI display used for direct visual demonstration.


2. Main Task

(1) Research RGB565/RGB888 image formats, display scanning timing, grayscale conversion, binarisation, Sobel edge detection, and FPGA video-stream processing; define the overall technical route and verification criteria.

(2) Define a unified pixel-stream interface containing pixel_data, pixel_valid, x_pos, y_pos, line/frame indicators, and frame_start, so that all processing modules can be connected using the same timing convention.

(3) Design an image input module. The baseline version shall read a pre-stored image from ROM by address; the extended version may support camera or host-computer input while preserving the same pixel-stream output.

(4) Implement grayscale conversion and thresholding. The module shall accept RGB pixels, output an 8-bit grayscale value and a binary result, and verify the fixed-point formula Gray=(77R+150G+29B)>>8 against a software reference.

(5) Develop a 3x3 sliding-window generator using two line buffers and shift registers. The design shall output nine aligned neighbouring pixels and include clear handling for image boundaries.

(6) Implement Sobel convolution and threshold decision logic. Compute Gx and Gy in parallel, use |Gx|+|Gy| as an approximate gradient magnitude, and generate valid edge pixels with controllable threshold.

(7) Design target coordinate statistics and display overlay logic. The circuit shall calculate the minimum/maximum x-y coordinates of edge pixels and draw a bounding box over the output image.

(8) Construct module-level and system-level testbenches. Compare RTL outputs with MATLAB/Python reference results at pixel or frame level, then verify board operation, display stability, resource utilisation, and timing performance.


3. Expected Outcomes

Deliverables include a synthesizable Verilog/SystemVerilog RTL codebase covering image input, grayscale conversion, window generation, Sobel detection, target annotation, display control, and key/button configuration. A verification report will include reference-model comparisons, error statistics, waveforms, FPGA resource utilisation, timing analysis, and board demonstration evidence. Finally, a graduation thesis will present the image-processing theory, fixed-point design, hardware pipeline architecture, verification method, health-and-safety considerations, and experimental results.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Background

When one object is imaged under a light microscope, the typical pictures obtained are the projection (2D) of the 3D object. During this process, the projected image loses information of the object due to the loss of depth. So directly recovering 3D information from a single 2D projection is an inherently ill-posed problem. However, when the exact shape and physical dimensions of the object are known in advance—such as a rectangular platelet with dimensions 5 × 5 × 2 μm—the reconstruction task transforms fundamentally. It is not a free-form shape generation problem anymore but becomes a well-constrained pose estimation problem, where only the six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) position and orientation need to be recovered. This prior eliminates scale ambiguity, resolves occluded backside geometry, and enables metric reconstruction from a single viewpoint. Despite this theoretical advantage, manual or classical fitting methods are slow and often fail under noise, overlapping objects, or ambiguous views. Recent advances in deep learning offer the ability to learn robust image-to-pose mappings, while physical models of image formation and motion dynamics can enforce consistency. This project sits at the intersection of computer vision, applied AI, and experimental microscopy, aiming to create a practical pipeline for high-throughput 3D tracking of micro-objects with known geometry.


Research Objectives

The goal of this project is to develop and validate an AI-assisted framework that reconstructs the full 3D pose of micro-sized objects with known shape and size from 2D microscopic images or video sequences. The specific objectives are:

  1. To construct a synthetic data generator based on a differentiable microscopy simulator that renders physically realistic images of the known object (e.g., a rectangular parallelepiped) under arbitrary 3D poses, while accounting for defocus, diffraction, and noise.
  2. To design a lightweight convolutional neural network that directly regresses the 6-DoF pose from a single cropped particle image, and to evaluate its accuracy and robustness compared to iterative geometric optimization.
  3. To incorporate temporal information by building a Bayesian filter (e.g., Unscented Kalman Filter or particle filter) that fuses per-frame pose estimates with a Brownian motion dynamic model, thereby resolving momentary pose ambiguities and generating smooth, physically plausible trajectories.
  4. To validate the entire pipeline on simulated test data and, if feasible, on real microscopic video of Brownian particles dispersed in an aqueous solution, comparing the measured translational and rotational diffusion coefficients with theoretical predictions as a quantitative benchmark.


Expected Outcomes

By the end of this project, we expect to deliver a modular software pipeline capable of processing raw microscopy images/videos and outputting 3D position and orientation trajectories for each target object.

Project Background

Traditional two-layer federated learning faces challenges such as high communication pressure, poor adaptation to Non-IID data, and insufficient security. Hierarchical federated learning (HFL) introduces edge servers to form a client-edge-cloud three-tier architecture, which improves efficiency but also expands the attack surface. Malicious clients or edge nodes can launch poisoning attacks, causing model drift or performance collapse. Existing methods lack a multi-level defense mechanism and cannot effectively resist collaborative attacks in hierarchical scenarios. Therefore, this project studies a robust hierarchical federated learning method based on gradient correction and time-series anomaly detection to ensure security, convergence, and usability.

Main Tasks

  1. Summarize research status of hierarchical federated learning, poisoning attacks, and defense mechanisms.
  2. Study the Multi-Timescale Gradient Correction (MTGC) framework and its role in alleviating Non-IID drift.
  3. Design a two-tier defense mechanism:
  • Edge-side: Trust evaluation based on cosine similarity to filter malicious updates.
  • Cloud-side: EWMA time-series monitoring to detect abnormal edge groups.
  1. Implement a complete hierarchical federated learning prototype system.
  2. Conduct experiments on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10 under IID/Non-IID and attack scenarios.
  3. Evaluate accuracy, robustness, overhead, and defense effectiveness.
  4. Write a complete graduation thesis.

Expected Outcomes

System

  • A prototype system of robust hierarchical federated learning with edge-cloud defense
  • Modules: local training, gradient correction, aggregation, anomaly detection, attack simulation
  • Visualization tools for accuracy, loss, defense effect
  • Complete experimental scripts, datasets, and result data

Graduation Thesis

  • System architecture diagrams, algorithm flowcharts, defense models
  • A large number of comparison charts and security analysis
  • Complete references and format specifications

Fixed differential privacy mechanisms fail to adapt to diverse client data distributions, leading to either excessive noise (low accuracy) or insufficient protection (privacy leakage).   3. Design an adaptive differential privacy mechanism for federated learning.

Federated learning allows multiple participants to train a joint model without sharing raw data, but model parameter updates may still be tampered with or forged during transmission and aggregation. Traditional federated learning lacks an effective mechanism to verify the correctness and integrity of global and local model updates. Homomorphic hash supports limited homomorphic operations on hash values and can be used to verify the correctness of aggregated results efficiently. Therefore, this project aims to design a verifiable federated learning system based on homomorphic hash to ensure model integrity, authenticity, and verifiability of the aggregation process.

  1. Study federated learning workflow, parameter aggregation, and security threats.
  2. Investigate homomorphic hash algorithms and their verification properties.
  3. Design a system architecture that supports verifiable aggregation using homomorphic hash.
  4. Implement local model training, hash generation, encrypted upload, aggregation, and public verification.
  5. Test model accuracy, verification efficiency, and tamper resistance.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

In high-speed Serializer/Deserializer (SerDes) communication systems, signal integrity and link reliability are paramount. Bit Error Rate (BER) is the most critical metric for evaluating link quality. Due to the high cost of external bit error rate testers, embedding a BERT logic within the physical coding sublayer is a standard industry practice. Pseudo-Random Binary Sequences (PRBS) are widely used for this purpose because their spectral characteristics closely mimic true random data while remaining entirely deterministic and repeatable. Designing a pure RTL-based PRBS test system allows for on-chip link validation, which is essential for link training, system debugging, and channel performance evaluation.


2. Main Task


(1) Research the mathematical principles of PRBS generation, focusing on the characteristic polynomials and LFSR architectures for standard PRBS-7, PRBS-15, and PRBS-31 patterns.

(2) Design a dynamically configurable, multi-mode PRBS generator supporting seamless switching between PRBS-7, 15, and 31 modes via register control.

(3) Develop a PRBS synchronization detector that utilizes sliding bit-by-bit comparison and seed-loading mechanisms to automatically achieve phase alignment with the incoming data stream, ultimately outputting a stable sync-lock indicator.

(4) Design a robust bit-error comparison and statistical module capable of performing bit-level error counting, block error counting, and cumulative BER calculations, incorporating wide-bit counters to support extended operational periods without overflow.

(5) Develop a highly automated testbench capable of simulating both error-free and noise-injected channel environments. The testbench must execute automated simulations for no less than 1,000,000 bit cycles to thoroughly verify the synchronization capture mechanism and the accuracy of the error statistical module.


3. Expected Outcomes

A fully synthesizable Verilog RTL codebase encompassing the multi-mode PRBS generator, the synchronization detector, and the comprehensive error statistics module.

A detailed simulation verification report presenting synchronization capture timing diagrams and statistical accuracy metrics under various injected bit error rates.

A comprehensive graduation thesis detailing the mathematical foundations of LFSRs, the synchronization algorithm architecture, simulation waveform analyses, and a comprehensive evaluation of the system's BER detection capabilities.
rows.themeTitle: RTL Design of a Multi-Mode PRBS Bit Error Rate Test (BERT) System for High-Speed SerDes Links

1. Research Background

The open-source, concise and customizable RISC-V architecture has become a mainstream research direction for embedded processors. Traditional single-cycle CPUs suffer from low instruction throughput and limited operating frequency, which cannot meet the efficiency requirements of embedded systems. Pipelining divides the instruction execution process to realize parallel operation and improve processor performance. However, pipelined circuits inevitably encounter data hazards and control hazards, so corresponding solutions are required. This work designs a lightweight 5-stage pipelined RV32I processor based on FPGA. Hazard elimination modules and basic peripherals are integrated for functional verification. The designed processor features low resource consumption, good portability and scalability, and is applicable to lightweight embedded scenarios.


2. Main Research Tasks

1. Build the data path and control path of a 5-stage pipeline (Instruction Fetch, Instruction Decode, Execute, Memory Access, Write-back) based on the RV32I integer instruction set.

2. Adopt data forwarding and pipeline stall mechanisms to resolve data hazards, and design branch processing logic to mitigate control hazards.

3. Integrate UART, GPIO, timer and other peripherals to construct a complete on-chip minimal SoC system.

4. Conduct functional simulation with Modelsim, and verify the correctness of instructions via assembly and C test programs.

5. Complete hardware debugging on FPGA development boards, and analyze resource utilization, operating frequency and overall performance.


3. Expected Results

(1) Deliverables

1. Compilable Verilog RTL source code, simulation testbench and constraint files.

2. Simulation waveforms, timing reports and resource utilization analysis reports of the pipeline system.

3. Complete test cases (assembly & C programs) and corresponding operating results.

4. Full graduation project thesis.

(2) Demonstration Results

1. A standalone pipelined CPU soft core running on FPGA, supporting arithmetic, logic, jump and memory access instructions.

2. On-board demonstrations including LED control via GPIO, serial port output and timer operation, to verify the coordination of the processor and peripherals.

3. Performance comparison with single-cycle CPU, showing the advantages of pipeline architecture in instruction throughput and maximum operating frequency.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

In advanced high-speed SAR ADCs, particularly those utilizing redundant or sub-radix-2 architectures, capacitor mismatch inevitably degrades dynamic performance parameters such as ENOB and SFDR. Foreground digital calibration is highly effective for addressing this: the exact capacitor weights are mathematically estimated offline (training phase) and then utilized to digitally reconstruct the raw analog samples in real-time (inference phase). While the weight estimation can be handled by open-source software like the ADCToolbox, the real-time inference demands a dedicated on-chip digital backend. This project focuses on designing the pure RTL hardware accelerator necessary to execute this weight reconstruction continuously at high clock frequencies without disrupting the data stream.


2. Main Task

The core objective is to design and verify a high-throughput digital backend for a 12-bit sub-radix-2 SAR ADC. The quantified tasks include:

(1) Research the error mechanics of capacitor mismatch in redundant SAR ADCs and utilize the open-source Python ADCToolbox to process sample datasets, extracting the optimal calibrated digital weights.

(2) Design the RTL architecture for the real-time weight reconstruction module. This involves mapping the extracted weights into internal registers and constructing a fully pipelined Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) tree capable of calculating the sum of products (W_i * B_i) in real-time.

(3) Optimize the Verilog codebase to achieve high-frequency timing closure. For instance, design a 4-to-5 stage pipeline architecture to ensure the logic path can meet aggressive timing constraints (e.g., targeting a 1 GHz clock domain for an ASIC implementation, or maximizing the Fmax on an FPGA target).

(4) Develop an automated testbench that streams raw, uncalibrated binary data from the Python toolkit into the Verilog simulation environment, captures the reconstructed output, and feeds it back to the ADCToolbox to verify that the calibrated ENOB matches the software-only ideal results.

(5) Synthesize and implement the RTL design on an FPGA development board, demonstrating real-time data processing and valid resource utilization (Logic Elements/DSP blocks).


3. Expected Outcomes

Deliverables include:

- A fully synthesizable, deeply pipelined Verilog RTL codebase for the ADC digital reconstruction backend.

- A co-simulation framework bridging the Python ADCToolbox and the hardware Testbench, complete with spectral analysis graphs verifying ENOB and SFDR recovery.

- A comprehensive graduation thesis detailing the weight calibration theory, the RTL pipeline architecture, timing optimization strategies, and FPGA implementation results.

1. Background

Modern 10 Gigabit Ethernet (10GbE) utilizes IEEE 802.3 64b/66b line coding to achieve 96.97% transmission efficiency. Because 66 is not a power of two, a "Gearbox" module is required to handle non-integer bit-width conversions between the 66-bit line rate and 64-bit internal buses. This project focuses on the RTL design and verification of the 10GBASE-R Physical Coding Sublayer (PCS).


2. Main Tasks

The project implements four core modules:

- Encoder/Decoder: Design 64b/66b parsing logic for both data and control frames.

- Parallel Scrambler: Develop a Python script to automatically derive and generate Verilog RTL for a 64-bit parallel scrambler/descrambler using the polynomial G(x) = x^58 + x^39 + 1.

- Block Lock FSM: Design a state machine (HUNT, CHECK, LOCK) to manage sync header tracking and alignment.

- Gearbox: Implement TX (64-to-66) and RX (66-to-64) modules using wide buffer registers and phase accumulators.


3. Expected Outcomes

Deliverables include synthesizable Verilog RTL, the Python code-generation script, and a comprehensive testbench. System stability will be validated through closed-loop simulations, demonstrating zero bit errors across 10,000+ clock cycles under various traffic scenarios. A complete graduation thesis documenting the design architecture and waveform analysis will also be produced.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1.Background

The biological retina is a high-performance front-end visual processing system that can perform complex visual operations such as light adaptation, motion detection and direction selectivity under low power consumption. Direction selectivity refers to the selective response of ganglion cells to motion stimuli in specific directions, which acts as the core physiological mechanism for biological motion perception and visual analysis. Traditional image sensors separate the photosensitive unit from the signal processing unit, resulting in high power consumption, large signal delay and poor real-time performance. Such limitations hinder their application in low-power wearable devices and bionic robots. To solve this problem, this project intends to construct a bionic retinal direction-selective visual circuit to reconstruct the multi-layer neural pathway of the retina. In this research, organic photodetectors are used to simulate biological photoreceptors for photoelectric conversion. Analog circuits are designed to replicate the signal regulation and transmission characteristics of bipolar cells, starburst amacrine cells and direction-selective ganglion cells. This study realizes the native direction-selective function of the retina at the hardware level, providing a feasible design scheme for low-power bionic visual hardware.

2.Main Task

(1) Analyze the biological mechanism of retinal direction selectivity. According to the multi-layer neural structure of the retina, the physiological functions of photoreceptors, bipolar cells, starburst amacrine cells and ganglion cells are mapped into corresponding circuit modules to establish the overall system framework.

(2) Design and construct analog circuit units to simulate the signal transmission characteristics of bipolar cells and the lateral inhibition mechanism of amacrine cells. The motion filtering characteristics of ganglion cells are realized through circuit logic to complete the core direction-selective function and relevant simulation verification.

(3) Complete PCB design, fabrication and welding to build a hardware test platform. Moving optical stimuli in different directions are applied to test the circuit and verify the directional response performance of the system.

(4) Test key performance parameters including response speed, direction selectivity index and static power consumption. Combined with biological visual mechanisms, the circuit characteristics are analyzed to realize iterative optimization and debugging.

3.Expected Outcomes

(1) Establish a complete design scheme for the bionic retinal direction-selective circuit, complete circuit simulation of each functional module, and retain systematic simulation data and analysis results.

(2) Construct a hardware prototype integrating photodetectors and analog neural circuits, which realizes the selective response to moving optical stimuli in specific directions at the physical hardware level.

(3) Collect and organize measured system data, quantitatively analyze key indicators including direction selectivity index, response speed and power consumption, and evaluate the comprehensive performance of the bionic circuit.

(4) Compile a graduation thesis summarizing system design, circuit simulation, hardware construction and experimental tests. This work verifies the feasibility of replicating retinal neural visual functions through analog circuits and provides references for the design of similar bionic visual circuits.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Water load is a type of component to calibrate the power level in the microwave output system. As the output power of devices is improved, the water load is necessary to achieve the better heat dissipation and the larger power capacity.

In the water load design, some significant factors below have been taken into account:

 

1. For better power absorption and dissipation, the radio frequency characteristics of the water load, especially the field distribution and the reflection properties, must be simulated.

 

2. Due to the gyrotron operation characteristics, the input field should be TE11 mode.

 

3. Process difficulty, mechanical strength, and heat dissipation capacity should be balanced according to the dielectric sheet dimension selection.

 

4. Volume and weight should be miniaturized to achieve portability.

 

In this project, we will design and fabricate a novel 30-kW-class continuous wave (CW) portable water load for Ka-band microwave output system. Though this project, students can understand the meaning of reflection coefficient and loss coefficient, and have a more intuitive understanding of transmission systems such as waveguides.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1.Background


In daily photography, video surveillance, and forensic investigation, reflections caused by glass media (such as windows, picture frames, or mirrors) present a common yet challenging interference. This non-semantic reflection superposition not only severely degrades image visual quality but also obscures the real target objects behind the glass, leading to the failure of high-level vision tasks such as object detection and scene understanding. Traditional physical model-based reflection removal methods are limited by their prior assumptions and often suffer from insufficient generalization when dealing with complex, overlapping reflection layers. In recent years, deep learning, with its powerful capabilities in feature disentanglement and image reconstruction, has provided a new approach to separating reflection components from mixed images. Therefore, conducting research on deep learning-based glass reflection removal methods holds significant practical value for enhancing image clarity and improving the robustness of visual systems.

2. Main task


(1)  Analyze the causes of image glass reflection and the basic principles for its removal;


(2)  Collect paired datasets for reflection removal, such as Real915, and perform preprocessing;


(3)  Design a deep network model for reflection removal based on MPGInet's two-stage iteration;


(4)  Design loss functions and training strategies specifically for reflection removal, and conduct validation experiments and comparative analysis.


Technical Indicators:

(1)  PSNR>25dB

(2)  SSIM>0.8


3.Expected outcomes


（1）Bachelor's degree thesis.


（2）Glass reflection removal algorithm program based on deep learning.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Background

Understanding what a model does not know is a critical part of many machine learning systems. Today, deep learning algorithms are able to learn powerful representations that can map high dimensional data to an array of outputs. However, these mappings are often taken blindly and assumed to be accurate, which is not always the case and may cause disastrous consequences. In May 2016, there was the first fatality from an assisted driving system, caused by the perception system over-confidently confusing the white side of a trailer for bright sky [1]. Quantifying uncertainty in computer vision applications can be largely divided into regression settings such as depth regression, and classification settings such as semantic segmentation. Two inherently different sources of uncertainty, often referred to as aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty, can be distinguished [2]. Aleatoric (aka statistical) uncertainty refers to the notion of randomness, that is, the variability in the outcome of an experiment which is due to inherently random

effects, and hence cannot be reduced. As opposed to this, epistemic (aka systematic) uncertainty refers to uncertainty caused by a lack of knowledge of data, and can in principle be reduced with additional information. As such, separately estimating (disentangling) these two types of uncertainties is of great importance. A very recent study benchmarked uncertainty disentanglement methods in the classification setting [3]. However, research in disentangling aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties in the regression setting is still quite limited. In this project, we will focus on estimating (disentangling) these two types of uncertainties for deep learning regression problems.


References

[1] A. Kendall and Y. Gal, "What Uncertainties Do We Need in Bayesian Deep Learning for Computer Vision?," in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), vol. 30, pp. 5574-5584, 2017.

[2] E. Hüllermeier and W. Waegeman, "Aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in machine learning: an introduction to concepts and methods," Machine Learning, vol. 110, no. 3, pp. 457-506, 2021.

[3] B. Mucsányi, M. Kirchhof, and S. J. Oh, "Benchmarking Uncertainty Disentanglement: Specialized Uncertainties for Specialized Tasks," in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), vol. 37, 2024.


Main tasks

1) Literature reading. The student will read references recommended by the supervisor on uncertain estimation and disentanglement for deep learning regression models.

2) Method re-implementation. The student will re-implement the methods reported in the references by downloading the accompanying code and data and running them.

3) Comparison. The student will perform a systematic comparison across state-of-the-art methods to identify the comparative pros and cons of each approach.

4) Contribution. Upon completing all the aforementioned tasks, the student is expected to either refine existing approaches or adapt an established uncertainty disentanglement method to address a specific regression task, such as object detection.


Expected outcomes

A high-quality final-year project report that delivers an in-depth analysis of uncertainty disentanglement for regression problems, and ideally, incorporates novel refinements to existing approaches.
rows.themeTitle: Uncertainty disentanglement for deep learning regression

3) Implement a baseline deep learning model (e.g., an encoder‑3D decoder network) that takes the two X‑ray images as input and predicts the 3D voxel occupancy or segmentation mask for L3, L4, L5.

4) Train and evaluate the model on the prepared dataset. Quantify reconstruction accuracy using Dice coefficient (and optionally Hausdorff distance).

5) Visualise the reconstructed 3D vertebrae and analyse the results.

2) A processed dataset (CT sub‑volumes with corresponding biplanar DRR images) for L3‑L5.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
This project integrates a binocular‑vision‑based master‑end handle tracking system with a slave‑end robotic manipulator (equipped with a force sensor) to form a complete teleoperation prototype for remote ultrasound scanning. The binocular system not only estimates the 6‑DOF pose of the simulated ultrasound handle but also monitors the axial pressure applied by the operator’s hand against the desktop (e.g., by detecting vertical displacement or deformation of a compliant pad). The slave‑end robot, which holds an ultrasound probe, follows the master’s pose while regulating contact force based on the measured axial pressure and the slave’s force sensor readings. The student will develop a unified control strategy that combines pose tracking and force control, implement the whole system, and validate its performance in simulated ultrasound tasks.


The student will be required to:

1) Integrate the binocular pose tracking module and the slave‑end robotic arm control module into a single software framework (e.g., ROS). Establish low‑latency communication between the master and slave ends.

2) Extend the control strategy to include force regulation:

Use the binocular system to estimate the axial pressure applied by the master handle.

Read the real‑time force signal from the slave‑end force sensor (mounted on the robotic wrist or probe).

Implement a hybrid control scheme (position‑force) where the slave robot follows the master’s pose while maintaining a desired contact force (e.g., force‑tracking impedance control or direct force control).

3) Perform system‑level experiments: an operator moves the master handle to guide the slave robot over the phantom. Collect quantitative metrics: pose tracking error, force tracking error, end‑to‑end latency, task success rate, and subjective operator feedback.

4) Analyse the stability and usability of the integrated system, and propose possible improvements.


Expected Deliverables:

1) Complete integrated teleoperation software including master pose/force estimation, slave control, and communication.

2) Demonstration video of the prototype performing at least two different scanning tasks on a phantom.

3) Performance evaluation report and graduation thesis.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Surgical navigation systems rely on multimodal medical imaging for precise anatomical localization. However, intraoperative 3D imaging remains challenging due to spatial constraints and technical limitations in operating rooms. This project focuses on deep learning-based approaches to achieve real-time 2D-3D registration between intraoperative bi-planar X-ray images (e.g., anterior-posterior and lateral views) and preoperative CT scans. Compared to single-view methods, bi-planar X-ray provides complementary geometric constraints, which can significantly improve registration accuracy and robustness.


The student will be required to:

1) Curate and preprocess CT datasets, including intensity normalization and spatial alignment.

2) Master cone-beam CT projection geometry and implement Digitally Reconstructed Radiograph (DRR) algorithms that support bi-planar projections (e.g., AP and lateral views).

3) Reproduce state-of-the-art deep learning models for 2D-3D medical image registration (e.g., CNN-based or transformer-based approaches), and extend the model to fuse informtion from bi-planar X-ray images (e.g., via two-stream networks or feature-level fusion strategies).

4) Enhance baseline models through architectural improvements or training strategies, followed by comprehensive validation using clinical metrics (e.g., registration error, success rate, computational time).


Expected Deliverables:

1) Deep learning codebase for 2D-3D registration with bi-planar X-ray input (GitHub repository)

2) Preprocessed CT dataset and simulated bi-planar DRR dataset

3) Quantitative evaluation report (comparison with single-view baselines)

4) Technical report and graduation thesis

rows.themeProjectDescription:
This project focuses on high‑fidelity 3D reconstruction of small industrial components (e.g., plastic gears, metal shafts) using Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), which leverages NeRF’s strengths in geometric accuracy and appearance preservation (color, texture, gloss). Experiments are conducted in a calibrated offline environment with known camera poses. The student will build a multi‑view capture rig, acquire images under controlled lighting, and train a NeRF model (e.g., using Nerfacto in Nerfstudio) that directly reads pre‑calibrated camera parameters (bypassing COLMAP pose estimation). The final reconstruction will be evaluated both geometrically (Chamfer distance, completeness) and in terms of appearance fidelity (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS on novel views). Results will be compared with those from one or more classical reconstruction techniques (e.g., Structure‑from‑Motion with Multi‑View Stereo, or volumetric fusion) to provide a broader benchmark. Defect detection is not required, but the potential for quality inspection may be discussed.


The student needs:

1) Build a multi‑view image capture platform (turntable with a single camera or a small camera array) and accurately calibrate all camera intrinsics and extrinsics using a calibration board. Acquire multi‑view images of at least two industrial components (≥60 views per component) under typical lighting conditions (e.g., uniform illumination and a single directional light).

2) Implement a NeRF reconstruction pipeline using an open‑source framework (e.g., Nerfstudio with the Nerfacto model). Modify the data loader to directly read the pre‑calibrated camera parameters, bypassing any structure‑from‑motion step. Train the model to obtain a dense 3D representation.

3) Quantitatively evaluate geometric accuracy: if a CAD model or a high‑precision scan is available, align the extracted mesh with the ground truth and compute Chamfer distance and surface completeness. Otherwise, use view‑synthesis metrics on held‑out test views as an indirect proxy.

4) Quantitatively evaluate appearance fidelity: render the NeRF model at specified camera poses (including both training and held‑out views) and compare the rendered images with the real images using PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS.

5) Compare the NeRF results with those of the other reconstruction techniques in terms of geometric accuracy and appearance fidelity. Summarize the complementary strengths of the two methods.


Expected Deliverables:

1) Complete NeRF reconstruction and evaluation codebase (GitHub repository), including camera calibration, data loading, model training, geometry evaluation, and appearance evaluation scripts.

2) Calibrated multi‑view image dataset (with camera parameters) for at least two industrial components.

3) Reconstructed NeRF models (mesh or point cloud) and rendered novel views.

4) Technical report and graduation thesis.

The final 3D models will be evaluated quantitatively in terms of geometric accuracy (Chamfer distance, if a CAD model is available, or view‑synthesis metrics such as PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) and rendering quality. The student needs:

2) Acquire multi‑view images of at least two different industrial components (≥30 views per component) and organize the data with the pre‑calibrated camera parameters.

3) Study the fundamental principles of Gaussian Splatting, focusing on the key differences between 2DGS (surface‑oriented) and 3DGS (rendering‑oriented) in terms of geometry reconstruction and surface extraction.

4) Implement the data loading module to directly read pre‑calibrated camera parameters into an open‑source Gaussian Splatting framework (e.g., Nerfstudio with gsplat library, or the official 2DGS/3DGS codebases), bypassing any structure‑from‑motion step. 1、Background

Humanoid robots are increasingly deployed in complex environments requiring agile, precise, and compliant movements—such as service robotics, healthcare assistance, and industrial collaboration. The joint actuation system directly determines a humanoid robot's dynamic performance, energy efficiency, and safety. Permanent magnet synchronous motors (PMSMs) have become the dominant choice for joint drives due to their high torque density, fast dynamic response, and low rotor losses. However, achieving smooth, high-precision servo control under varying loads, limited joint space, and real-time constraints remains challenging. Classical PID control often fails to handle nonlinearities, parameter uncertainties, and external disturbances common in legged or bimanual manipulation tasks. Therefore, developing advanced yet practical servo control methods for PMSM-based humanoid robot joints is both academically meaningful and critical for real-world robot autonomy.

2、Project Content

This project focuses on designing, analyzing, and validating improved servo control strategies for a PMSM-driven robot joint. First, a mathematical model of the PMSM in the

dq-rotating reference frame is established, including electromagnetic torque and mechanical load dynamics. Then, a cascaded field‑oriented control (FOC) architecture is adopted as the baseline. To enhance tracking precision and disturbance rejection, two candidate methods are investigated: (1) a sliding mode controller (SMC) with a continuous approach law to reduce chattering while maintaining robustness, and (2) a model‑based active disturbance rejection controller (ADRC) that estimates and compensates lumped disturbances in real time. All controllers are first designed and tuned in MATLAB/Simulink, incorporating practical constraints such as current limits and PWM update delays. A hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) simulation using a commercial robot joint module is planned for validation. Key performance metrics include step response overshoot, settling time, torque ripple, and trajectory tracking accuracy under dynamic loads. The final deliverable includes a comparative analysis of the proposed methods and a guideline for implementing the superior solution on embedded motor controllers for humanoid robots.

3、Expected Outcomes

1）A complete simulation model of the ANPC-based ESS grid-connected converter with MPC in MATLAB/Simulink.

2）Demonstration that MPC achieves faster dynamic response and lower current THD (e.g., <3%) than conventional PI control.

1.Background


Laser drilling is a typical application in the field of laser processing, playing an irreplaceable role in precision manufacturing such as film cooling holes on aeroengine turbine blades and micro-holes on fuel injectors. The rotary dual prism, as a precision beam deflection device, achieves beam pointing control by rotating two prisms with the same wedge angle relative to each other. This project aims to explore the fast positioning algorithm of dual optical wedges based on the equivalent vector model and its application in laser drilling, providing theoretical and technical support for enhancing the positioning performance of laser processing.
